scope.scopeNotesMd: This report compares the local R4 and R6 core `StructureDefinition/Meta` snapshots and differentials, plus the value sets bound directly by `Meta.security` and `Meta.tag`. It treats `Meta.versionId`, `Meta.lastUpdated`, `Meta.source`, `Meta.profile`, `Meta.security`, and `Meta.tag` as local elements. Inherited `Element` members (`Meta.id`, `Meta.extension`) and package-wide model infrastructure changes are recorded as out of scope rather than as local findings.
outOfScope: The R6 baseDefinition changed from `Element` to `DataType`; this appears to be the package-wide datatype hierarchy shift and is excluded from local `Meta` findings under the inherited/base-artifact rule.
Inherited `Element` content on `Meta.id` and `Meta.extension`, including condition propagation and extension constraint representation, is excluded from findings for `Meta`.
FHIR-wide removal of `ElementDefinition.constraint.xpath` from snapshot constraints is excluded as a global definition-format/tooling issue, not a local `Meta` content-model change.
Normative status metadata, work-group metadata, generated narrative XHTML, publisher/contact wording, and package publication metadata are not treated as instance-breaking `Meta` changes.
Search parameters, operations, profiles, implementation guides, validator-specific behavior, and resource-level uses of `Resource.meta` outside the base datatype definition are outside this report.

narrativeReportMd:
# Meta R4→R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
No local hard instance-breaking change was found for `Meta`: the canonical identity, element names, cardinalities, datatypes, summary flags, modifier flags, and direct reference target for `Meta.profile` are stable. The material migration concerns are semantic/runtime changes in `Meta.lastUpdated` and `Meta.source`, plus an R6-to-R4 terminology conformance risk for `Meta.security`.

## Scope
The assessment is scoped to the `Meta` datatype itself and its locally declared elements. Inherited `Element`/`DataType` hierarchy behavior, `Meta.id`, `Meta.extension`, XPath constraint representation, and package-wide class hierarchy changes are excluded from local findings.

## Main migration themes
R6 gives more explicit and more permissive guidance for server-managed metadata. `lastUpdated` is no longer described as effectively always populated after creation and may be out of sync with visible content changes. `source` is broadened from a source system/entity-oriented URI to a more general data-source URI that can identify portions of a structure or an agent-like source. The `security` binding still points to `ValueSet/security-labels` with extensible strength, but that value set now includes the broader v3 Confidentiality value set rather than only the v3 ConfidentialityClassification subset.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact item is the `Meta.security` terminology change because R6 security labels can include confidentiality concepts that R4 terminology checks may not treat as members of the R4 security-labels value set. This is not a JSON/XML shape break, but it can affect privacy/security policy enforcement and cross-version validation.

## Findings requiring human review
The terminology finding should be reviewed with an official terminology expansion and current THO package because the local R6 package includes the `ValueSet/security-labels` compose but not the referenced external terminology artifacts.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Most R6 changes are clarifications or semantic widenings rather than removals. The least backward-compatible piece is the broadened security-label value set composition; preserving a fixed R4 subset or supplying a clear cross-version ConceptMap would make R6-to-R4 conversions more predictable.

## Follow-up analysis
Follow-up should be delegated to the `DataType`/`Element` infrastructure reports for the base-definition shift and to terminology analysis for `ValueSet/security-labels`, `ValueSet/common-tags`, and the referenced THO value sets/code systems.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: No local hard instance-breaking changes were found in `Meta`. The main concerns are changed `lastUpdated` server behavior, broadened `source` semantics, and a `security` value-set composition change that can affect R6-to-R4 terminology conformance. Confidence is high for structure/cardinality/type stability and medium for terminology impact because local R6 terminology expansions were not available.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration is mostly about metadata semantics rather than instance shape. Existing R4 `Meta` JSON/XML can still be structurally represented in R6, but client synchronization logic should not assume `lastUpdated` is always populated or exactly tracks visible content changes. Provenance logic should treat `Meta.source` as a broader data-source indicator. Cross-version security label handling should test values from the broader v3 Confidentiality code system against R4 validators and policy engines.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: The StructureDefinition comparison gives high confidence that no local element was added, removed, renamed, moved, or cardinality/type narrowed. Confidence is lower for terminology severity because the local R6 package does not include authoritative expansions of the referenced external THO value sets; the terminology finding relies on the ValueSet compose change and R4 bundled code-system content.

findings.title: Meta.lastUpdated guidance is relaxed and now permits out-of-sync timestamps

oldState.summary: Optional `instant` element whose comment said the value is always populated except when the resource is first being created.

semanticText.short: When the resource version last changed
semanticText.definition: When the resource last changed - e.g. when the version changed.
semanticText.comment: This value is always populated except when the resource is first being created. The server / resource manager sets this value; what a client provides is irrelevant. This is equivalent to the HTTP Last-Modified and SHOULD have the same value on a read interaction.

oldState.narrativeMd: In R4, the element was optional by cardinality but the explanatory text set a strong operational expectation: after initial creation, server-managed resources normally have `meta.lastUpdated`, and clients could treat it as closely aligned with HTTP `Last-Modified`.

newState.summary: Same optional `instant` element, but R6 says submitted instances generally omit it, server population is conditional, and timestamps MAY be out of sync with visible content changes.

semanticText.short: When the resource version last changed
semanticText.definition: When the resource last changed - e.g. when the version changed.
semanticText.comment: This element is generally omitted in instances submitted in a PUT or POST. Instead, it might be populated by the server when data is received or assigned when crafting the instance when constructing a response. The value MAY be out of sync with visible resource changes in either direction.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 keeps the same wire shape but changes implementer expectations. It explicitly allows cases where visible resource content changes without changing `lastUpdated`, and cases where `lastUpdated` changes without visible content changes.

facts.oldValue: Always populated except when first being created; client-provided value is irrelevant.
facts.newValue: Generally omitted in PUT/POST; server might populate it; MAY be out of sync with visible changes.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not a structural validation break because `Meta.lastUpdated` remains `0..1 instant`. The breaking risk is behavioral: cache invalidation, polling, synchronization, optimistic refresh logic, and audit heuristics that used the R4 wording as a guarantee can be wrong against R6 servers that legitimately omit or desynchronize the timestamp.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The main risk is stale or over-frequent synchronization rather than direct clinical data loss. In systems where `lastUpdated` controls privacy-filtered feeds or audit workflows, the business impact can be higher and should be assessed locally.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify real server behavior for server-managed timestamps, facades, privacy filtering, and internally generated resources.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the R4 expectation as a strong SHOULD while adding narrowly scoped exceptions for facades, privacy filtering, and generated resources.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal is reasonable: `lastUpdated` is server-managed metadata, and the R6 text documents real cases where visible resource bytes and infrastructure update times diverge. There is no wire-format break, but the semantic weakening can affect R4-era synchronization and cache logic. With a partial less-breaking wording available, the change is probably justified only because the alternative would leave an unreliable guarantee in the base specification.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base R6 design could have retained R4's expectation that `meta.lastUpdated` is normally populated after creation and aligned with HTTP Last-Modified, then added explicit exception language such as 'SHOULD update for visible changes unless the server documents a facade, privacy, or generated-resource limitation.' That would preserve more client assumptions for ordinary REST servers, but it would not fully meet the R6 goal for systems whose metadata genuinely cannot track visible content changes in both directions.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Less disruptive for clients that poll by timestamp, but it would only cover common server cases and could overpromise behavior that some R6 servers cannot guarantee.

evidence.detail: R4 says the value is always populated except when the resource is first being created.
evidence.quote: This value is always populated except when the resource is first being created.

evidence.detail: R6 says submitted instances generally omit the element and lists cases where lastUpdated may be out of sync with visible content changes.
evidence.quote: Unless specified otherwise, this element MAY be out of sync with changes in either direction.

evidence.detail: R4 cardinality and type are 0..1 instant.
R6 cardinality and type remain 0..1 instant.

examples.examplesMd: A client that polls for updates by comparing only `meta.lastUpdated` can miss an R6 facade-server content change if the visible resource content changes but the server's `lastUpdated` value does not. Conversely, it can reprocess unchanged visible content if privacy or internal-data changes update `lastUpdated`.

findings.narrativeMd: `Meta.lastUpdated` did not change shape, but its operational contract changed materially. R4's text supported the common assumption that server-returned resources normally carry a timestamp that tracks version changes. R6 explicitly allows legitimate gaps between timestamp changes and visible resource changes, which can surprise sync, cache, and audit implementations even though the same JSON is still valid.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4-valid instance does not become invalid in R6 because the element remains optional and has the same primitive type. Valid R6 content is also structurally representable in R4. The compatibility issue is runtime/conformance behavior: applications that elevate the R4 comment into a hard invariant may reject or mishandle R6 server responses or update interactions.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review any logic that treats `meta.lastUpdated` as mandatory after creation, as a complete change detector, or as exactly equivalent to visible-resource modification time. Prefer server-supported history, `_lastUpdated` search semantics, ETags/version ids, subscriptions, or domain-specific reconciliation where exact change detection matters. Test omitted, unchanged, and changed `lastUpdated` scenarios during R6 migration.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The same clarification could have been presented as non-normative implementation guidance while preserving R4's stronger expectation, but that would leave clients with an unreliable guarantee. The R6 wording is more honest for facades, generated resources, and privacy filtering, at the cost of weakening assumptions used by older clients.

findings.title: Meta.source semantics broaden from source system to general data source

oldState.summary: Optional `uri` identifying the source system of the resource and corresponding to `Provenance.entity.what[x]`.

semanticText.short: Identifies where the resource comes from
semanticText.definition: A uri that identifies the source system of the resource. The source may identify another FHIR server, document, message, database, etc.
semanticText.comment: In the provenance resource, this corresponds to Provenance.entity.what[x].

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 frames `Meta.source` primarily as a source-system or source-entity URI. Implementations could reasonably map it to a `Provenance.entity.what[x]`-style source.

newState.summary: Same optional `uri`, but it identifies the data source more generally, can refer to portions of a structure, and may correspond to either `Provenance.entity.what[x]` or `Provenance.agent.who[x]`.

semanticText.short: Identifies where the resource comes from
semanticText.definition: A uri that identifies the data source of the resource. It can also refer to portions of a structure, such as a section, segment, row, etc.
semanticText.comment: The source may correspond to Provenance.entity.what[x] or Provenance.agent.who[x], though it may be a more general or abstract reference.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 broadens the intended referent. A valid source URI might identify a database row, document section, segment, abstract data source, or agent-like origin rather than a FHIR server or Provenance entity.

facts.newValue: may correspond to Provenance.entity.what[x] or Provenance.agent.who[x], or a more abstract reference

impact.impactRationaleMd: The element remains a single optional `uri`, so structural validation is unchanged. The risk is semantic: R4 consumers may interpret an R6 `Meta.source` URI too narrowly as a source system or Provenance entity, while R6 producers may send more granular or agent-like identifiers that existing policy, deduplication, or provenance mapping code did not expect.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Misinterpreting source metadata can affect provenance display, routing, or trust decisions, but the element remains a minimal provenance hint rather than the full provenance record.

justification.inferredGoal: Permit `Meta.source` to describe real-world data origins that are not whole FHIR servers or simple Provenance entities.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `Meta.source` limited to a source-system or source-entity URI and add a separate optional base element for row, segment, section, or agent-like source detail.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal is reasonable because lightweight metadata often needs to identify feeds, rows, segments, sections, or agent-like origins without requiring a full Provenance resource. The change does not invalidate R4 instances, but it broadens the meaning of an existing URI that R4-era code may treat as a system or Provenance entity identifier. A less-breaking base design is possible, but its duplication and ambiguity costs are material, so the chosen simplification is probably justified rather than clearly avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would keep `Meta.source` with the R4 source-system/source-entity meaning and add a new optional R6 element, such as a source detail or source target choice, for structural portions and agent-like origins. That would let old assumptions about `Meta.source` remain valid while still giving R6 a place for more granular origin metadata. The tradeoff is permanent model complexity: producers could populate either or both fields for closely related origin facts, consumers would need precedence rules, and the newer detail would still need separate handling when converting to R4.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 source-system assumptions, but creates two same-resource places for origin facts and requires precedence, mapping, and validation rules.

evidence.detail: R4 defines the element as identifying the source system of the resource.
evidence.quote: A uri that identifies the source system of the resource.

evidence.detail: R6 defines the element as identifying the data source and allows references to portions of structures.
evidence.quote: It can also refer to portions of a structure, such as a section, segment, row, etc.

evidence.detail: R6 allows correspondence to Provenance.entity.what[x] or Provenance.agent.who[x], or a more general/abstract reference.

examples.examplesMd: The fragment is syntactically representable in R4 because `Meta.source` is still a `uri`. The risk is semantic: a granular row-level source is explicitly anticipated by R6 but may violate R4-era assumptions that the value names a source system or a Provenance entity.

findings.narrativeMd: `Meta.source` was semantically widened. R4 consumers that parse this field as a system identifier, server identifier, or direct `Provenance.entity.what[x]` link may encounter R6 values that identify smaller structural components or agent-like origins. That can affect provenance mapping and trust/routing code even though validators still see the same URI type.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: No R4-valid instance becomes invalid in R6 due to this change, and R6 values are still syntactically representable in R4. Compatibility risk appears when business rules treat the URI namespace or target kind as constrained by the R4 wording.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Audit code that classifies `Meta.source` values, maps them automatically to `Provenance.entity.what[x]`, or assumes they identify only whole systems. For cross-version transforms, preserve the URI but consider adding full `Provenance` when the distinction between entity, agent, or structural portion matters. Test representative server, document, row/segment, and abstract-source URI forms.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The broadening could have been made less surprising by retaining the R4 source-system wording and adding explicit extensions for source portions or agent-like origins. The R6 approach is simpler and more flexible but shifts interpretation burden to consumers.

findings.title: Meta.security security-label value set broadens from ConfidentialityClassification to full Confidentiality

oldState.summary: `Meta.security` is `0..* Coding` with an extensible binding to `ValueSet/security-labels`; in R4 that value set included `v3-ConfidentialityClassification` for confidentiality labels.

binding.description: Security Labels from the Healthcare Privacy and Security Classification System.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The R4 compose includes `http://terminology.hl7.org/ValueSet/v3-ConfidentialityClassification`, which the local R4 package defines as the six concepts `U`, `L`, `M`, `N`, `R`, and `V` from `CodeSystem/v3-Confidentiality`, plus the other security-label component value sets.

oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 security-labels value set used the confidentiality-classification subset for confidentiality codes. That subset is narrower than the whole v3 Confidentiality code system.

newState.summary: `Meta.security` still uses `0..* Coding` and the same extensible binding URL, but the R6 `ValueSet/security-labels` compose includes the broader `v3-Confidentiality` value set.

binding.description: Security Labels from the Healthcare Privacy and Security Classification System.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: No official expansion was run. The listed codes are inferred from the R4 bundled v3 Confidentiality CodeSystem concepts that are outside the R4 `v3-ConfidentialityClassification` value-set compose and appear included when R6 references the broader `v3-Confidentiality` value set.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 leaves the element and binding URL unchanged but changes what the bound value set includes for confidentiality. R6 producers may use more specific confidentiality/access/sensitivity labels than the R4 security-labels value set enumerated.

facts.note: The canonical binding URL did not change.

facts.newValue: Broader v3 Confidentiality value set, including additional access-kind, information-type, and modifier concepts.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The `Meta.security` element and binding URL match exactly across versions. The finding compares the local ValueSet resources resolved by that binding URL in each package rather than a changed ElementDefinition binding field.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4-to-R6 is a widening, so existing R4 confidentiality classification codes remain within the broader R6 value-set intent. R6-to-R4 is riskier: an R6 `Meta.security` label using a confidentiality code outside R4's `ConfidentialityClassification` subset may be flagged by R4 terminology validators, ignored by R4 policy engines, or require local policy mapping. Because the binding is extensible rather than required, this is usually a conformance/semantic risk rather than a hard JSON validation failure.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Security labels influence access control, privacy filtering, and obligation handling. Losing or flattening a more specific R6 confidentiality label during R4 conversion can have privacy or policy consequences even when the instance remains syntactically valid.

justification.inferredGoal: Make the all-security-labels value set include the full v3 Confidentiality family rather than only the confidentiality-classification subset.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable for R4-to-R6 compatibility: R4 `Meta.security` codings remain structurally valid, and the reported risk is broader R6 labels in reverse-direction terminology or policy handling.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal is coherent because an all-security-labels value set can reasonably include the broader v3 Confidentiality family. The existing R4 element shape, binding URL, binding strength, and confidentiality-classification codings are preserved for R4-to-R6 use. The material concern is that R6 instances may use additional confidentiality labels that R4 validators or policy engines do not recognize, which is a reverse-direction terminology and policy risk rather than a breaking R4-to-R6 base-design issue.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: For R4-to-R6 compatibility, no backward-compatible alternative is needed because R4-valid `Meta.security` content is still representable. A design that kept the R4 confidentiality-classification subset under the existing canonical and introduced a new broader value set would help some R6-to-R4 validators, but it would fragment the terminology surface and would address down-conversion rather than avoiding an R4-to-R6 break. ConceptMaps and local security-label policies are migration mitigations, not backward-compatible base R6 alternatives.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base alternative is needed; retaining the R4 subset or adding a second value set would mainly trade R6 expressiveness for easier R6-to-R4 conversion.

evidence.detail: R6 `Meta.security` keeps the same extensible binding URL.
The R4 bundled `v3-ConfidentialityClassification` value set enumerates confidentiality classification codes U, L, M, N, R, and V.
The R4 bundled v3 Confidentiality CodeSystem also contains additional selectable concepts such as B, D, I, ETH, HIV, PSY, SDV, C, S, and T that are outside the R4 classification subset.

examples.examplesMd: The `ETH` example is syntactically a valid `Coding` in both versions, but it is inferred to be inside the broader R6 `security-labels` compose and outside the R4 confidentiality-classification subset. The migration example shows one possible local policy of preserving the specific code while adding a broader R4 classification code; whether `R` is appropriate requires policy review and should not be applied blindly.

findings.narrativeMd: The `Meta.security` element itself is stable, but the value set behind its extensible binding is broader in R6. This matters because security labels are often interpreted by terminology-aware validators and access-control engines, not just by FHIR structural parsers. R6 data can carry more specific confidentiality/access/sensitivity labels that an R4 system may not recognize as part of the R4 all-security-labels set.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances using the six confidentiality classification codes remain compatible with R6. The reverse direction is less clean: an R6 instance using a broader v3 Confidentiality code can be represented as a `Coding` in R4, but an R4 terminology validator or policy engine may warn, reject under local strictness, or fail to enforce the intended label. The extensible binding prevents this from being classified as a universal hard instance break.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4 conversion, do not drop unfamiliar security labels. Preserve the original coding where possible and use a site-approved policy map to add an R4 confidentiality classification code only when the mapping is safe. Test security-label validation and access-control behavior with broader v3 Confidentiality codes such as `ETH`, `HIV`, `S`, and `T`. A ConceptMap or local policy table is likely needed for production migration.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The broadening is understandable for an 'all security labels' value set, but changing the compose behind the same canonical URL makes cross-version behavior less predictable. A new broader value set or an explicit R4/R6 ConceptMap would have been easier for backward-compatible migration, though at the cost of more terminology artifacts and less uniform R6 expressiveness.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Confirm with an official R6 terminology expansion and current THO package before treating the listed added codes as exhaustive. Security policy owners should review mappings; this is not only a technical code-system issue.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: Canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, derivation, active status, and abstract flag are stable. The direct baseDefinition change is explicitly out of scope as a DataType hierarchy issue.
No local `Meta` element was added, removed, renamed, moved, split, or merged. Snapshot element ids match across R4 and R6.
All local element cardinalities remain unchanged: `versionId`, `lastUpdated`, and `source` are `0..1`; `profile`, `security`, and `tag` are `0..*`.
Local element datatypes are unchanged: `id`, `instant`, `uri`, `canonical(StructureDefinition)`, and `Coding` remain in the same locations.

Binding strengths and canonical value-set URLs for `Meta.security` and `Meta.tag` are unchanged. The `security-labels` value-set compose changed and is reported as a finding; `common-tags` changed only under an example binding and is reported as a notable non-breaking change. Official expansions were not available locally.

Local FHIRPath constraint expressions on local elements remain the inherited `ele-1` rule. XPath metadata removal and inherited `Meta.extension` constraint representation are out of scope global/inherited definition-format changes.
No fixed value, pattern value, or default value was found on local `Meta` elements in either version.
No local minValue, maxValue, maxLength, or regex limit changed or appeared.
No local `Meta` element is a modifier in either version.
Summary flags for all local elements are stable; the local metadata elements remain included in summaries.
No local slicing was added or changed. Inherited `Meta.extension` slicing is out of scope for this artifact.
No local element path, primitive/complex representation, choice naming, or JSON/XML serialization shape changed.

There is no new local R6 element or datatype that is structurally unrepresentable in R4. The main reverse-direction limitation is semantic/terminology conformance for broader security-label and source semantics.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Common Tags example value set now includes v3 ObservationValue SUBSETTED
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: `Meta.tag` remains `0..* Coding`, the binding strength remains `example`, and the binding URL remains `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/common-tags`. Example bindings do not constrain instance validity, so adding `v3-ObservationValue#SUBSETTED` does not make old data invalid or require new data to use that code.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Terminology pick lists, generated enums for example values, or UI suggestions may now include `SUBSETTED`. Cross-version systems should preserve the coding if encountered; R4 can structurally carry it even though the R4 example value set did not include it.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Specification metadata and generated narrative changed without changing the datatype identity
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: R6 updates publication metadata such as package version, publisher, work-group extension, generated narrative, jurisdiction, and `experimental=false`, while preserving the canonical `StructureDefinition/Meta` identity and content model. These changes affect documentation and package metadata rather than instance shape.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Tools that diff raw StructureDefinition JSON should filter publication metadata and generated XHTML when looking for instance-impacting changes.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Binding-definition metadata extensions were added to terminology bindings
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: R6 adds `http://hl7.org/fhir/tools/StructureDefinition/binding-definition` extensions to the `Meta.security` and `Meta.tag` ElementDefinition bindings, but the instance elements, binding strength, and binding URL do not change. This affects definition consumers, not FHIR instances using `Meta`.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: StructureDefinition-consuming tools should tolerate additional ElementDefinition extensions and should not interpret them as changes to the instance content model.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: R6 `Meta` now derives from `DataType` instead of directly from `Element`. Per scope rules this class-hierarchy change should be owned by the `DataType`/base datatype analysis rather than by this `Meta` report.

Inherited `Meta.id`/`Meta.extension` differences, condition propagation, and inherited `ele-1`/extension constraint representation should be analyzed with `Element` and related infrastructure artifacts.

The `Meta.security` finding depends on terminology compose and expansion differences. A terminology-focused analysis with current THO artifacts should confirm added/removed codes and any ConceptMap guidance.
`Meta.tag` has an example binding whose compose now includes `v3-ObservationValue#SUBSETTED`. This is non-breaking for `Meta`, but terminology/UI tooling may want a cross-version note.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No official R4→R6 diff or ballot change note was used. The conclusions are based on local computable package artifacts and direct comparison.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Review the official FHIR R6 change log or datatype diff pages for `Meta` when available.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The local R6 package contains the `ValueSet/security-labels` and `ValueSet/common-tags` compose definitions but not all referenced external terminology artifacts or authoritative expansions. The `Meta.security` added-code analysis is therefore inferred, not expansion-verified.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Run R4 and R6 expansions against the appropriate terminology packages/THO versions and compare selectable codes, including abstract/notSelectable handling.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No matrix of real R4 and R6 validator behavior was executed. Extensible-binding severity can vary by validator configuration and terminology availability.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Validate representative R6 security-label examples against common R4 validators with strict, warning, and terminology-unavailable configurations.

crossArtifactPatternsToCheck: Resources or interactions that rely on `Resource.meta.lastUpdated` for synchronization
Profiles or policy engines that constrain `Meta.security` security labels
Cross-version transforms that preserve or map broader v3 Confidentiality codes
